The '''DBAR problem''', or the <math>\bar{\partial}</math>-problem, is the problem of solving the [[differential equation]]
<math display="block">\bar{\partial} f (z, \bar{z}) = g(z)</math>
for the function <math>f(z,\bar{z})</math>, where <math>g(z)</math> is assumed to be known and <math>z = x + iy</math> is a [[complex number]] in a [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]] <math>R\subseteq \Complex</math>. The operator <math>\bar{\partial}</math> is called the DBAR operator:{{sfn|Ablowitz|Fokas|2003}}
<math display="block">\bar{\partial} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} + i \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \right)</math>
The DBAR operator is nothing other than the complex conjugate of the operator
<math display="block">\partial=\frac{\partial}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} - i \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \right)</math>
denoting the usual differentiation in the complex <math>z</math>-plane.

The DBAR problem is of key importance in the theory of [[integrable systems]], [[Schrödinger equation|Schrödinger operators]] and (together with a jump condition) generalizes the [[Riemann–Hilbert problem]].{{sfn|Ablowitz|Fokas|2003}}{{sfn|Haslinger|2014}}{{sfn|Konopelchenko|2000}}
